In plain words

The article introduces TATS, a tool that helps researchers watch and understand how sign-in tokens move between Microsoft cloud services and other web systems. It matters because the author found that some Microsoft tokens were accepted in places that did not match where they were supposed to be used, and that tokens could be created before multi-factor authentication was completed. Organizations using Microsoft cloud services may be affected if their access rules do not explicitly require multi-factor authentication for related services, leaving gaps that an attacker could abuse.

Summary
TATS is an open-source tool for collecting, decoding, and visualizing OAuth token exchanges, with special support for Microsoft cloud behaviors like brokered client IDs and FOCI. Early use revealed Microsoft token audience mismatches and a Conditional Access gap where pre-MFA tokens can sometimes be exchanged for access to nested services that lack explicit MFA policies.

The article introduces Token Analysis and Tracking System, or TATS, a tool for collecting, storing, decoding, analyzing, and visually tracking OAuth token exchanges. The author built it after finding manual token tracking in Burp slow, tedious, and difficult to scale during research into Microsoft cloud token behavior. TATS is intended for research and education, and it was designed to account for known OAuth deviations in the Microsoft ecosystem while also working with any OAuth implementation.

TATS can ingest data from Burp exports, live Chrome DevTools Protocol browser tracking, and mitmproxy files, then display token activity in a database-backed web GUI. The interface includes a summary dashboard, token inventory, refresh token exchange view, Microsoft-specific FOCI and BroCI sections, and graph and sequence visualizations. It can also enrich token information with application data from entrascopes, redact selected claims, and optionally store full token values for export and command generation.

Using TATS, the author found cases where tokens with an audience claim for management.core.windows.net were presented to resources such as management.azure.com or portal.azure.com. The author also found that refresh and access tokens were issued before MFA was completed, and that an Azure Portal token without MFA in its authentication method claim could be exchanged for a key vault token when the key vault did not have an explicit Conditional Access Policy requiring MFA. When the author created a new Conditional Access Policy and repeated the exchange, the policy blocked access, showing that relying only on Microsoft’s MFA requirement for admin portals can leave gaps for nested applications.

  • TATS became significantly more useful when it moved from static Burp exports to live Chrome DevTools Protocol and mitmproxy capture, because this allowed token information to appear nearly live and better handled browser and web socket activity.
  • The article shows that relying on Microsoft’s mandatory MFA requirement for admin portals can still leave gaps, because related nested applications such as key vault may need their own explicit Conditional Access Policies requiring MFA.
  • The audience mismatch tracking in TATS exposed cases where tokens appeared to be used against hosts that did not match the token’s stated audience, which the author describes as contrary to expected OAuth behavior.
  • The `--store-tokens` option is intentionally disabled by default because storing full token values improves export and command generation but increases the sensitivity of the collected database.
Key Points
  • 01TATS is a tool that collects, stores, decodes, analyzes, and visually tracks OAuth token exchanges, with support for known OAuth deviations in the Microsoft ecosystem and other OAuth implementations.
  • 02TATS can ingest token data from Burp exports, live Chrome DevTools Protocol browser tracking, and mitmproxy files, then display the results in a web GUI backed by a database.
  • 03The TATS web interface includes a summary dashboard, token inventory, refresh token exchange tracking, Microsoft-specific FOCI and BroCI views, and graph and sequence visualizations of token exchanges.
  • 04Using TATS, the author observed tokens with the audience claim management.core.windows.net being presented to resources such as management.azure.com or portal.azure.com.
  • 05The author found that tokens could be issued before MFA was completed and that an Azure Portal token without an MFA authentication method could be exchanged for a key vault token when the key vault lacked an explicit Conditional Access Policy requiring MFA.

Cisco Talos uncovered a ClickFix-style cryptocurrency theft campaign that tricks users into pasting malicious JavaScript into Chrome or Tampermonkey, then uses Google Sheets’ Visualization API as C2 to inject a web skimmer. The script replaces legitimate crypto deposit addresses and clipboard contents with attacker-controlled wallets while displaying fake bonus offers.

Cisco Talos tracked a cryptocurrency-stealing campaign that used ClickFix-style social engineering to persuade targets to run malicious JavaScript in their own browser sessions. The lures posed as leaked reports of nonexistent API flaws at cryptocurrency swap services that would supposedly increase trade payouts. Early versions instructed users to paste code into Chrome’s address bar, while later versions instructed them to install the Tampermonkey extension and add a script that persisted when visiting SimpleSwap.

The first-stage script retrieved obfuscated payload components from a publicly published Google Sheets document through Google’s Visualization API, then assembled and injected them into the targeted site. The resulting web-skimming script altered transaction interfaces, replaced legitimate deposit addresses in browser responses and copied clipboard data with attacker-controlled Bitcoin addresses, and displayed fake bonus-related interface elements. Talos identified 49 Bitcoin wallets associated with the campaign; 24 of 30 commonly used addresses received a combined 0.159 BTC, approximately $10,000 at early August 2026 valuations, and the actors repeatedly restored components after disruption by changing Google Sheets, Google Docs, or paste.sh content.

  • The campaign shifted from asking users to run code once in Chrome’s address bar to using Tampermonkey, allowing the malicious script to run again whenever the victim visited the targeted trading site.
  • Google Sheets’ publicly accessible Visualization API let the attackers deliver changing payloads through normal browser requests to docs.google.com, making the activity resemble legitimate web traffic.
  • The attackers concealed payloads in the spreadsheet by formatting text as white on a white background and moving hidden cells farther down as they added revisions.
  • After reported campaign components were blocked, the operators restored the operation within about a week by switching to a new Google Sheet and paste.sh script.

The Italian volunteer tech collective Autistici/Inventati is shutting down after the U.S. government labeled it a terrorist organization, which quickly led to its website domain being suspended and its bank account being frozen because others feared penalties for working with it. The group had provided privacy-focused email, websites, mailing lists, blogs, video tools, and other online services for thousands of users, who now have to back up their data and may lose long-running online homes. Summary
Italian privacy-focused tech collective Autistici/Inventati says it will shut down after the U.S. designated it a terrorist organization, triggering sanctions risks, domain suspension, and loss of banking access. The move raises broader concerns in Europe about U.S. control over internet infrastructure and the vulnerability of non-commercial privacy services to political sanctions.

Italian technology collective Autistici/Inventati announced Sunday that it will shut down operations after the U.S. government declared it a terrorist organization and imposed sanctions. The volunteer-run collective, founded in 2001, provided free privacy-focused services including about 16,000 email addresses, 1,500 websites, 5,500 mailing lists, and a network of around 10,000 blogs. The State Department labeled A/I an “extremist group” operating infrastructure for “far-left militants across the world,” while the collective said the designation was unjust and arbitrary.

The designation had immediate operational effects on the collective’s infrastructure and finances. The U.S.-based Public Interest Registry suspended the group’s .org domain on August 28, and the Italian bank Banca Etica suspended its account over sanctions risks while saying it condemned the use of OFAC listings for political purposes. A/I said it would instruct users on how to back up content from blogs, mailboxes, and websites because it could no longer maintain its mission of offering secure and non-commercial digital tools under the circumstances.

The shutdown affects users who relied on A/I as an online home, including people with long-running blogs on the Noblogs platform. Digital rights advocates and supporters said the case raises concerns about European sovereignty, U.S. influence over internet infrastructure, and the precedent for non-commercial hosts, registrars, and privacy-preserving services. Anne Roth, a digital policy advisor in the German Parliament, said the response showed how internet governance structures can fall apart after a U.S. designation made without a judicial procedure.

  • The sanctions had practical effects almost immediately through private infrastructure providers, with the .org domain operator and the collective’s bank taking action within two days of the State Department designation.
  • The State Department’s action affected a large user base beyond the accused political groups, including about 16,000 email addresses, 1,500 websites, 5,500 mailing lists, and 10,000 blogs hosted by the collective.
  • The case shows how dependence on U.S.-linked internet governance can affect European services, since a U.S.-based domain registry suspension helped disrupt an Italian collective’s operations.
  • Banca Etica’s response highlighted the pressure sanctions create for service providers, as it suspended the account over risk while publicly condemning the political use of OFAC listings.
  • Long-running user content became difficult to manage even when still readable, as Anne Roth said her nearly two decades of Noblogs posts remained online but she could not access the administration tools.
Key Points
  • 01Italian technology collective Autistici/Inventati announced it will shut down after the U.S. government declared it a terrorist organization and imposed sanctions.

Summary
A targeted salary-increase phishing email used only trusted infrastructure, chaining Microsoft SafeLinks and Google open redirects to an abused third-party host while hiding the victim’s email address in a split base64 URL path. The key takeaway is that clean link scans and email authentication passes can still miss credential-harvesting attacks when attackers borrow legitimate services and reputation.

A national sales director at a fresh produce and food manufacturing company received a fake internal HR email about a salary increase. The visible message was sparse, using the company name, the recipient’s full name, and a single “Visit Portal” button to imply a legitimate salary portal notice. The message was sent from a real mailbox at a small law firm unrelated to the recipient’s company, and the landing page was hosted on a British production company’s domain that was also unrelated to the lure.

The button led through four hops: an Outlook SafeLinks rewrite, a Google Meet linkredirect endpoint, a Google URL redirector, and then a final host on the unrelated production company’s domain. No attacker-registered domain appeared anywhere in the chain, and all five extracted links returned scanner verdicts of clean or not applicable. The final host used autodiscover as both a subdomain label and path segment, making the destination look like Microsoft mail configuration plumbing while serving a salary-themed phishing lure.

The final URL path included the recipient’s own email address encoded in base64 and split across tilde-separated chunks, allowing per-victim tracking and personalization while avoiding simple checks for plaintext addresses or obvious base64 blobs. The message initially failed SPF and DMARC from a Lithuania-geolocated hosting IP, but a later hop passed authentication through Microsoft 365 even though DKIM was absent and the sending domain’s DMARC policy was none. The article says the decisive detection came from the recipient reporting the message himself, after which an analyst confirmed it as phishing.

  • The absence of any attacker-owned domain made domain age and reputation checks largely ineffective, because every visible host in the chain belonged to Microsoft, Google, or an unrelated legitimate business.
  • Splitting the base64-encoded recipient address across separator characters can evade simple detections that look for either plaintext email addresses or continuous base64 strings in URLs.
  • A delivery-time authentication pass did not prove the message content was trustworthy, because DKIM was absent and the sending domain’s DMARC policy was set to take no action on failures.
  • Near-invisible filler text was used to dilute the message’s statistical fingerprint while remaining hidden from the recipient, showing why the visible email body alone may not reflect what filters evaluate.
  • The recipient’s manual report was decisive even though link scanners marked the extracted links clean or not applicable, highlighting the value of user reporting when trusted infrastructure is abused.

  • 03The final URL used an `autodiscover` subdomain and path segment and included the recipient’s own email address encoded in base64 and split across tilde-separated chunks.

Russian national Sergei Filimonov was extradited to the U.S. to face fraud and identity theft charges over an alleged bank account takeover scheme that used spoofed banking pages and sponsored search links to steal credentials. Russian web developer Sergei Anatolyevich Filimonov was extradited from the Republic of Georgia to the United States to face an indictment tied to a multimillion-dollar bank account takeover scheme. He appeared in an Atlanta federal court on September 4 and pleaded not guilty to fraud and identity theft charges. U.S. authorities said he remains in custody.

Prosecutors allege that from November 2023 through October 2025, Filimonov and others used spoofed domains and fraudulent login pages to target online banking customers. They allegedly bought sponsored search-engine links to divert customers to fake login pages and steal their credentials. Authorities said the stolen credentials were then used to access bank accounts, review balances, and initiate unauthorized wire transfers.

The case is linked to the December 2025 federal seizure of web3adspanels.org, which investigators said held login credentials for thousands of victims. As of that announcement, the FBI had identified at least 19 victims, with attempted losses of about \(28 million and confirmed losses of roughly \)14.6 million. Filimonov faces charges including conspiracy to commit bank and wire fraud, access device fraud conspiracy, bank, wire, and access device fraud, and aggravated identity theft, with a possible sentence ranging from a minimum of two years to a maximum of 175 years in prison.

Censys says many Internet-connected industrial machines, such as equipment used in substations, pump houses, remote well sites, and water systems, are connected through consumer or mobile networks. That can make it hard for researchers to find the actual utility, manufacturer, or operator responsible for fixing a risky device, because the address may only point to a phone company. This matters because attackers have targeted exposed controllers in water and wastewater systems, locking operators out or disconnecting equipment, which led to boil-water notices and manual operation.

Summary
Censys found that about 70% of 134,000 Internet-exposed ICS hosts sit on consumer and mobile networks, making it hard to identify and notify the organizations responsible for securing them. This exposure notification gap leaves critical infrastructure devices visible to attackers but difficult for defenders to trace and remediate.

Censys reports that approximately 70% of the roughly 134,000 Internet-exposed industrial control system hosts it observes globally are on consumer and mobile networks. The article says this creates an exposure notification gap because registration data for mobile-connected equipment often points to the telecommunications provider rather than the organization operating the device. As a result, researchers may be able to see an exposed device but may not have a reliable way to identify and notify the owner responsible for securing it.

The article says this gap matters because industrial control systems are used in environments such as substations, pump houses, remote well sites, and unstaffed automation sites where cellular connectivity may be the best or only option. It cites a July 30, 2026 CISA alert warning that threat actors were targeting Internet-exposed PLCs in water and wastewater systems. According to CISA, attackers accessed exposed controllers, changed passwords to lock operators out, and altered device IP addresses to disconnect them, leading to boil-water notices and extended periods of manual operation.

Censys observes an average of 134,000 distinct hosts running ICS services and tooling exposed on the Internet in early 2026, up roughly 4% from about 129,000 in 2024. North America accounts for more than 38% of global ICS exposure, while the United States alone accounts for 32% with over 40,000 exposed hosts.
